records.description: Bioceb (European Master in Biological and Chemical Engineering for a Sustainable Bioeconomy) is a 2-year Erasmus Mundus Joint Master (120 ECTS) run by a consortium including Aalto University, AgroParisTech and other partner universities, training future research and innovation managers for the bioeconomy. The programme includes compulsory mobility of at least two study periods in two countries. Erasmus Mundus scholarship holders receive a monthly subsistence allowance of 1,400 euros for the entire duration of the programme, paid for a maximum of 24 months and capped at 33,600 euros per student, with participation costs covered. Bioceb is entitled to approximately 12 scholarships per cohort out of 50 across the project duration.

records.applicant_utility: Applicant utility (original writing for the Bioceb Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Scholarships): budget on the published envelope rather than on vague promises - scholarship holders receive a 1,400 euro monthly subsistence allowance for the full programme duration, capped at 24 months and 33,600 euros, and the participation costs are covered, so the money side is solid but the selection is extremely selective with cohorts capped at 25 students. English is the hard gate: only the official tests count (IELTS Academic overall 6.5 with 6 in Writing, or TOEFL iBT overall 92 with 22 in Writing, Home Edition accepted), so book a test early enough for results to arrive before the January deadline. The application is file-based rather than interview-based, so the motivation letter (typically 1-2 pages, addressed to the consortium, linking your studies to career plans) and the two ranked study tracks carry most of the weight - justify the tracks against your academic background and goals. Note the compulsory mobility: at least two study periods of 30 ECTS in two countries different from your country of residence, so choose tracks with that structure in mind. Results arrive in April, and an appeal procedure exists if you believe an eligibility or selection decision was unfair.

records.description: The France-South Africa Scholarship Programme is a selective programme of the French Embassy to South Africa, co-funded with South African partners, directed to citizens of South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi who intend to study for a Master's degree or PhD at French higher education institutions, with start of studies in September 2027. Laureates receive a monthly living allowance of 900 euros (Master's) or 1,850 euros (PhD), a return flight ticket and France Excellence scholarship-holder status, but tuition fees are not covered. Applications for the 2027 cycle closed on 8 October 2026; shortlisted candidates are announced from early December 2026 and the final award is confirmed in four waves between May and July 2027.

verification.notes: Verified on the official programme website and rulebook on 10 October 2026: 900 euro monthly allowance for Master's and 1,850 for PhD students (subject to reassessment), return flight ticket, France Excellence status components (social security and health insurance, priority housing, visa-fee exemption, CVEC exemption, Campus France support, conditional enrolment-fee exemption at public universities applying standard national rates), CAF housing support of approximately 150 euros per month, tuition not covered, eligibility (born on or after 1 January 1997, SA/Lesotho/Malawi citizenship, 60% minimum average), 2027 timeline (21 July - 8 October 2026, interviews November 2026, shortlist from early December 2026, final selection in four waves May-July 2027), French courses February-July 2027 via Alliances Françaises, and the priority STEM fields.

records.applicant_utility: Applicant utility (original writing for the France-South Africa Scholarship Programme): the single most useful planning fact is the sequence - applications close 8 October, but acceptance into a French programme only needs to be proven between February and July 2027, so you can (and should) apply for the scholarship before you hold an admission offer. Build the file around a ranked list of up to three programmes, each with its webpage, application dates and fees, so the panel can see that your plan is realistic inside the French calendar. The money covers the essentials but not tuition: 900 euros per month for Master's (1,850 for PhD), one return ticket, social security and health insurance, priority housing, visa-fee exemption, CVEC exemption and conditional enrolment-fee exemption at public universities that apply the standard national rates, plus possible CAF housing support of about 150 euros. For PhD applicants the decisive element is the supervisor commitment letter, and co-supervision is favoured, so establish contact with a French host early. If your work sits in the published priority fields - digital technologies, AI, quantum, biotechnology, health, environmental sciences, energy, low-carbon mobility, space, food systems or ICT - make that alignment explicit, and use the February-July 2027 French courses to prepare for study in France.
